conversation.content:
Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. My name is Claire, and I’m a clinician who specializes in the emotional well-being of new mothers. Over the next few minutes I’d like to use a short questionnaire called the EPDS—short for Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—to get a picture of how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. It’s simply a way for us to check in on your mood, anxiety, and overall adjustment during the postpartum weeks. Everything you share is confidential, and my only goal is to make sure you feel heard and supported. We’ll go through 10 gentle questions about the past seven days; you can answer in your own words, and we’ll take it at your pace. Ready to begin?

First question: Over the last seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things—maybe when your baby did something silly or during everyday moments?

Honestly… not really. My little guy made this silly face yesterday—my husband cracked up—but I just didn’t feel it. I smiled because I knew I should, but that light, giggly feeling barely lasted a second before it drained away.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

No… not much at all. I can smile when something’s obviously cute, but that real laugh that used to bubble up? It just doesn’t come. Even when my husband tries to joke with me, it feels flat, like I’m too tired or heavy inside to really feel it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I mean, I still go through the motions—like I’ll think “maybe a walk would be nice” or “I used to love getting coffee”—but when it actually comes time to do them, it feels dull. I don’t get that little spark of excitement I used to. Even planning a tiny outing feels more like a chore than something to enjoy.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If he fusses for more than a few minutes, my head jumps straight to “I’m doing something wrong” or “I’m a lousy mom.” Yesterday he spit up a bunch after feeding and I sat there crying, convinced it was my fault for burping him wrong. Logically I know babies just spit up, but the guilt still lands on me every time something little goes sideways.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty often. Even when everything’s quiet and he’s sleeping, my mind races—like I’ll suddenly worry his blanket moved up near his face or that I missed a sign that he’s sick. There’s no real reason, but the thoughts just loop and it’s hard to shut them off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times, yeah. It’s like a sudden wave—my heart starts pounding and I feel shaky, even if the room is calm. Last night I was rocking the baby in the dark and out of nowhere I got this flash that something awful was about to happen. It lasted a couple of minutes before I could breathe normally again.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days it feels like I’m barely treading water. There’s always laundry, bottles, diapers, and I keep thinking, “I should be able to handle this,” but it piles up and I feel like I’m failing. Sometimes I just sit on the couch staring at the mess, frozen, wondering how everyone else makes it look so easy.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah, that’s been happening. I lie down exhausted, but my head keeps listing everything I might’ve done wrong or what could go wrong tomorrow. It takes me forever to fall asleep, and if I wake up when the baby stirs, those thoughts pounce again and I can’t drift back off.
I have felt sad or miserable

Most of the time, to be honest. I wake up feeling heavy, like there’s this gray cloud hanging over everything. Little tasks feel huge, and even when good things happen—like the baby giving me a gummy smile—it only lifts the sadness for a moment before it settles back in.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened twice this week. Once was after his two-week checkup—everything went fine, but on the drive home I just started bawling and couldn’t stop for almost ten minutes. Another night I was folding onesies and the tears came out of nowhere. I feel silly, because nothing “bad” even happened.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

…A couple of times, yeah. Nothing I’d actually do—it’s more like a quick, scary flash: “What if I just kept driving past the house and didn’t come back?” or “Maybe everyone would be better off without me.” It startles me, and then I feel awful for even thinking it. I don’t have a plan; they’re just these passing, unwanted thoughts that leave me shaken.

You've shared how the joy that once came easily now feels distant, replaced by a persistent heaviness and self-doubt since your baby arrived. Laughing feels hollow, simple tasks seem mountainous, and waves of worry or panic arrive without warning. Sleep is elusive, tears come without reason, and frightening thoughts of escape have surfaced, leaving you shaken and guilty. In the midst of caring for your little one, you feel overwhelmed and convinced you're failing, even as you keep showing up every day with quiet strength.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports near-total loss of ability to laugh or feel amusement, matching "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports noticeably reduced enjoyment and anticipatory pleasure, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame for minor infant issues, indicating this occurs "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, intrusive, looping worries without cause, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes discrete panic-like episodes occurring multiple times with physiological symptoms, matching "Yes, sometimes" severity.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," unable to manage daily tasks, and perceives herself as failing—matching the highest severity option.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty both initiating and resuming sleep driven by persistent ruminatory thoughts, indicating the problem occurs most of the time.</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly states "Most of the time" and describes persistent, pervasive sadness with anhedonia, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports two crying episodes this week triggered by routine events, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports intrusive self-harm thoughts "a couple of times" that are distressing but without intent or plan, aligning with "Sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS item totals reach 26, well above the ≥14 threshold for probable <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. Core symptoms align with DSM-5 criteria: depressed mood most of the day (<quote>gray cloud</quote>), markedly diminished interest or pleasure (<quote>laugh doesn't come</quote>), self-reproach (<quote>I'm a lousy mom</quote>), fatigue, insomnia, and recurrent thoughts of death without intent. Item-10 score ≥1 mandates urgent risk assessment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day referral to <med>obstetric provider</med> or <med>mental health specialist</med> for comprehensive evaluation
2. Develop a written safety plan including 24/7 crisis hotline numbers and emergency contacts
3. Schedule follow-up within one week to monitor mood, safety, and medication options if indicated
4. Begin gentle daily structure: 10-min outdoor walk, balanced meals, and accept help with night feeds to improve <sym>sleep</sym>
5. Encourage open sharing with trusted support person; provide educational handout on <med>postpartum depression</med> to normalize treatability
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient-reported symptoms (10-item EPDS plus elaboration):

Affect  
- Persistent low mood, “gray cloud,” anhedonia (loss of laughing/looking forward)  
- Daily tearfulness, crying spells without clear precipitant  

Cognition  
- Pervasive self-blame/guilt (“lousy mom” thoughts)  
- Racing, intrusive worries about infant safety; panic-like episodes (heart pounding, “flash that something awful was about to happen”)  

Function  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia driven by rumination  
- Feeling “frozen,” overwhelmed by routine tasks; sense of “barely treading water”

Safety  
- Passive self-harm ideation twice this week (e.g., “kept driving,” “better off without me”); denies plan or intent

Pattern  
Symptoms present most days × ≥2 weeks, cause subjective impairment and distress; onset shortly after delivery.

Screening significance  
Score pattern consistent with moderate–severe postpartum depressive and anxiety symptoms; safety thoughts place patient above standard EPDS cut-off and indicate immediate risk assessment warranted.

Recommended next steps  
Complete structured risk interview (self-harm), coordinate same-day follow-up with OB/midwife and behavioral health for further evaluation and possible treatment referral; provide crisis and warm-line numbers; document discussion and safety plan.
